n: This topic is devoted to the forensic medical examination of the bodies of fetuses and newborns, that is, chapter 10 of the textbook. The aim is to learn how to define the questions of the examination, the signs of newborn status and live birth, and the length of time the infant has lived. The outline is as follows: newborn status, live birth, gestational age, viability, duration of life, care and causes of death. Finally, the specific features of examining the body and the review questions are considered.

t: Circumstances in which an examination is carried out
n: First, let us establish when the examination is carried out. A forensic medical examination is ordered when the body of an infant whose mother is unknown is found. An examination is also carried out where delivery took place outside a medical institution and the child was stillborn. The same applies when there are complaints about the medical care given to a pregnant woman. The general condition is that there must be signs of violent death, or a suspicion of it.

Six specific questions are put in this type of examination, and they are given in groups. The first question: is the infant newborn; in forensic medicine this means the first 24 hours. The second: was it born alive; this is decided mainly by whether the infant breathed. Questions are also asked about fetal age and viability, how long the infant lived, and whether it was cared for. General questions are also put: the cause and time of death, the injuries and the mechanism by which they were inflicted. Attention: newborn status is 24 hours in forensic medicine, 4 weeks in paediatrics and 7 days in obstetrics. Do not confuse these.

t: The concept of newborn status across disciplines
n: The concept of newborn status in forensic medicine differs from that in paediatrics and obstetrics. In paediatrics, that is, the neonatal period, it is 4 weeks. In obstetrics and gynaecology it is 7 days. In forensic medicine this period is the first 24 hours after birth. This feature is closely tied to legislative requirements. Thus the meaning of the same term changes depending on the discipline, and the expert uses the forensic medical definition.

Let us look at the legal significance of newborn status. Article 99 of the Criminal Code applies where a mother deliberately kills her infant during birth or immediately after it. Because of pain and her psycho-emotional state, a mother may harm her child without being fully aware of what she is doing. In that case the act was committed by the mother, and the penalty is considerably milder. Article 97 applies to deliberate homicide committed by another person. Attention: there is a risk of error; the 4 weeks in paediatrics are not equal to the 24 hours in forensic medicine.

Case analysis. A delivery took place at home; the infant was found dead several hours after birth. Question: which concept applies, the 4 weeks of paediatrics, the 7 days of obstetrics or the 24 hours of forensic medicine? Answer: the forensic medical concept, that is, the first 24 hours. The infant is within this period and is therefore regarded as newborn. The next question: if the act was committed by the mother, is it Article 99, and if by another person, Article 97? Think this through yourself.

Blood stains and vernix caseosa. If there are no external injuries, blood stains on the body are a sign of newborn status; they form from tearing of the tissues of the birth canal. Blood stains lie on the surface of the body and disappear when washed. Vernix caseosa is a whitish-grey mass made up of secretion, epidermis, hair and amniotic fluid; it protects the fetal skin from maceration in the amniotic fluid. There is more of it in the skin folds, the axillae and the perineum, and if not washed off it persists for up to 1 week. Attention: blood stains are not blood from injuries. First establish that there are no external injuries, then assess the stain as a sign.

We distinguish caput succedaneum from cephalohaematoma. Caput succedaneum occurs with a narrow pelvis and weak labour; its cause is impaired circulation due to compression. It lies over the head, sometimes the buttocks; on section a reddish-yellow serous fluid is seen, and it is usually resorbed in 2-3 days. Cephalohaematoma is the result of birth trauma, a subperiosteal haemorrhage; it lies over one or several bones and is resorbed over 2 weeks or more. The main difference concerns the sutures: the swelling is also found over the projection of the sutures, whereas a cephalohaematoma is limited by the sutures. One is oedema of the soft tissues, the other is blood beneath the periosteum.

Meconium is called the first stool. It appears as a dark green or brownish-green, semi-liquid, homogeneous mass. Meconium is found in the large intestine, around the anus, and in the buttock and thigh regions. It contains mucus, bile pigments, intestinal epithelium, amniotic fluid and hair. Its composition changes with time and helps to determine fetal age. Attention: it is usually passed completely from the intestine in 1-2 days, but in premature infants this extends to 3-4 days.

Dynamics of umbilical cord changes. The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta. In a full-term infant it is 50-60 cm long and 1.5-2 cm thick. A fresh cord is moist, glistening and whitish-pink. In live birth the cord dries evenly: it shrivels, turns brownish-yellow, then brownish-black. At its base, after several hours, sometimes by the end of day 1, reactive inflammation appears, that is, the demarcation ring. On days 5-7 the cord separates along this ring.

t: Primary atelectasis; absolute and relative signs
n: Primary atelectasis is the state of lungs that have not breathed. Such an infant may live for a few seconds. There are three absolutely reliable, that is, absolute, signs: primary atelectasis of the lungs, absence of a ring on the cord or its initial signs, and an unseparated cord. The relative signs include blood stains, vernix caseosa, caput succedaneum and meconium. Attention: relative signs are not absolute; they may still be found on day 2 and later.

Quick questions. First question: how long is the newborn period in forensic medicine? Answer: the first 24 hours. Second question: which signs are absolutely reliable? Answer: primary atelectasis and the signs on the cord, that is, absence of the ring and an unseparated cord. Third question: how does caput succedaneum differ from cephalohaematoma? Answer: the swelling is also found over the projection of the intersutural lines; it is resorbed in 2-3 days. Fourth question: when is meconium completely cleared from the intestine? Answer: usually in 1-2 days; in premature infants up to 3-4 days.

t: Case analysis 2: signs of newborn status
n: Case analysis. On the body of a newborn there are vernix caseosa, traces of meconium and caput succedaneum. The cord is not separated from the body and the placenta. Question: which sign is absolutely reliable? Answer: the cord not separated from the body and the placenta, and also primary atelectasis of the lungs. Vernix caseosa, meconium and caput succedaneum are relative signs. They may be found on day 2 of life and later. Attention: there is a risk of error. The swelling is also found over the projection of the sutures, whereas a cephalohaematoma is limited by the bone.

Criteria of live birth. The criteria of the World Health Organization, that is, WHO: breathing, heartbeat, umbilical cord pulsation and voluntary movements. In forensic medicine, methods for determining heartbeat, cord pulsation and voluntary movement after death have not yet been developed. The question is therefore decided mainly by establishing whether the infant breathed or not. Quick question: by what methods is live birth determined? By tests, and by macroscopic, microscopic and laboratory examinations.

The lung test is associated with the names of Galen, Raugier and Schreyer. The specific gravity of lungs that have not breathed is 1.05–1.06, so they are heavier than water; lungs that have breathed are below 1.0. The procedure: first ligatures are placed on the trachea and oesophagus, and the organ block is placed in a vessel of water. If it sinks, the separate lungs are tested, then the lobes and pieces. If it floats, the test is stopped. A false positive result occurs with putrefaction, artificial respiration and freezing, and a false negative with secondary atelectasis. The test was first used in forensic practice by I. Schreyer in 1681.

t: Lung test: false results and the Taranukhin method
n: A lung that has breathed floats in water, with a specific gravity below 1.0; a lung that has not breathed sinks. Attention: putrefaction, artificial respiration and freezing may give a false positive, and secondary atelectasis a false negative result. If a piece of lung containing putrefactive gases is squeezed under water, it does not float up again. With artificial respiration the pieces do not float uniformly. A frozen lung that has been completely thawed sinks in water. In secondary atelectasis the Taranukhin method (1907) is used: in a flask under reduced pressure a piece of lung floats up.

The gastrointestinal test is associated with the name of Breslau (1865). When breathing, air passes through the oesophagus into the gastrointestinal tract. Air-containing areas float in water, and bubbles are released when they are punctured. In live birth air passes gradually, so the test also helps to estimate how long the newborn lived. Attention: with putrefactive gases and artificial respiration the test gives a false positive. In such cases its use is not recommended. The X-ray test (Dillon, 1939) cannot distinguish a lung that has breathed from artificial ventilation and putrefactive gases. It requires special equipment and is not used now.

The procedure for the gastrointestinal test. The test is based on the fact that during breathing part of the air passes through the oesophagus into the stomach and intestines (V. Breslau, 1865). First step: ligatures are placed on the inlet and outlet of the stomach, on areas of the intestine suspected of containing air, and on the rectum. Then the stomach and intestines are separated from the mesentery and placed in a vessel of water. Areas containing air float up, and bubbles are released when punctured under water. In live birth air passes gradually, so the test also helps to estimate how long the infant lived.

Macroscopic signs: let us compare the live-born and the stillborn. A lung that has breathed almost fills the chest and is elastic; when compressed, frothy blood is released. A lung that has not breathed is small, dense and lies close to the spine; little blood runs from the cut surface. In live birth the chest is barrel-shaped, the diaphragm is at the level of the 6th-7th rib, the lungs are marbled and uneven, weighing 85-90 g. In stillbirth the chest is flat, the diaphragm is at the level of the 4th-5th rib, the lungs are uniformly bluish dark red, weighing 55-60 g. Putrefaction in live birth begins in the respiratory organs, in stillbirth usually at the natural orifices.

Microscopic signs. In stillbirth the alveoli are not expanded, the epithelium is cuboidal, the septa are thick and there is no blood in the capillaries. In a lung that has breathed, the alveoli are expanded, the epithelium is flat, the septa are thinned and the capillaries are full of blood. Hyaline membranes consist of proteins, that is, albumin, globulin and fibrin; they are absent in a lung that has not breathed. In stillborn infants the pulmonary arteries have "bud-like" and "cushion-like" projections; after breathing they are absent.

Test yourself. Question 1: in forensic medical examination, the question of live birth is decided mainly by establishing which sign? Question 2: in the lung test, what is the specific gravity of lungs that have breathed and that have not breathed, relative to water? Question 3: if the lung test is false negative in secondary atelectasis, which method is recommended? Question 4: which test is no longer used in forensic practice, and why?

Case analysis. The putrefied body of a newborn was found. In the lung test, pieces of lung floated to the surface of the water. Question: does this result prove that the infant was born alive? How might putrefactive gases affect the result? Check: the floating pieces are squeezed by hand under water. If the gas is from putrefaction, they do not float up again. Attention: in putrefaction the gastrointestinal test also gives a false positive, so its use is not recommended.

t: Concepts of full term and maturity
n: The concepts of full term and maturity. Full term is a set of signs showing that pregnancy lasted on average 10 lunar months, or 280 days. Birth at term occurs at 37-42 weeks. A full-term infant is 50-54 cm long and weighs 3000-3500 g. Maturity, however, is a degree of physical development sufficient for life outside the mother's body: length of 45 cm or more and weight of 2500 g or more. Attention: full term and maturity are not the same. One rests on the duration of pregnancy, the other on physical development.

Let us calculate gestational age using formulae. Haase's formula gives age in lunar months of the fetus; the method of calculation differs in the first and second halves of pregnancy. In the first half the square root of the body length is taken, in the second half the length is divided by 5. Example: for 16 cm it gives 4 months, for 40 cm 8 months. The Baltazard-Derveaux index is 5.6; multiplied by the body length it gives gestational age in days: 40 cm × 5.6 = 224 days, that is, 8 months. In Yakupov's method (1981) the head circumference of the fetus is divided by 3.4 and the result gives the lunar month of the fetus: for 34 cm, 10 months.

t: Umbilical cord, placenta and ossification centres
n: Umbilical cord, placenta and ossification centres. According to Table 10.1, cord length in month VI is 38, in VII 42, in VIII 46, in IX 47, in month X 50 cm. Placental weight in month VI is 250, in VII 340, in VIII 410, in IX 470, in month X 500 g. Ossification centres: in the calcaneus in month V, 0.8–1.1 cm; in the talus in month VII, 0.7–1.0 cm; in the femoral epiphysis, that is, Béclard's centre, in month IX, 0.5–0.7 cm. Harmful habits delay the centres. In month VIII the swallowing reflex appears, and hair is found in the meconium.

Case analysis. The body of an infant whose mother is unknown was found; body length is 40 cm. The expert must determine gestational age. Haase's formula: in the first half of pregnancy the square root of the body length is taken, in the second half the length is divided by 5. Examples from the source: for 16 cm it is 4 lunar months, for 40 cm 8 lunar months. Baltazard-Derveaux: 40 cm × 5.6 = 224 days. Question: what is the gestational age in months of a fetus of 40 cm? Compare the result with the Baltazard-Derveaux index. In Yakupov's method the head circumference is divided by 3.4.

Viability of the infant. WHO criterion, that is, the World Health Organization: an infant less than 25 cm long and weighing less than 500 g is non-viable. The causes of non-viability fall into three groups: extreme prematurity, developmental malformation, for example anencephaly and a two-chambered heart, and birth trauma, that is, crushing of the brain and injury of the spinal cord. If an external malformation such as a sixth finger or cleft lip is found, the brain and organs are examined to exclude internal malformations. Attention: a live-born infant may also be non-viable.

t: Duration of life outside the mother's body
n: Let us consider the duration of life outside the mother's body along a timeline. At 1-2 hours hyaline membranes appear. At 5-6 hours air is in the small intestine and secondary atelectasis appears. By the end of day 1 the ring forms and meconium is passed. On days 2-3 the caput succedaneum is resorbed. If air is only in the stomach, the infant lived less than 3 hours; after 6 hours air passes into the large intestine. Jaundice develops on days 2–3 and resolves on days 1–10. Attention: these time frames are approximate, so in an examination as many signs as possible are taken into account.

t: Establishing whether the infant was cared for
n: Whether the infant was cared for is important for the legal assessment of circumstances in inquiry and investigation. External signs: the infant is swaddled, is wearing clothing, and the cord is cut and tied. If the body has been cleaned of blood stains and vernix caseosa, this also shows that care was given after birth. On internal examination, finding milk or a similar mass in the stomach also indicates care.

t: Case analysis 5: duration of life and care
n: Case analysis. In the body of a newborn, air was found only in the stomach and not in the intestines. At the base of the cord no demarcation ring is seen. If air is only in the stomach, the infant lived less than 3 hours. Air passes into the small intestine at 5-6 hours and into the large intestine after 6 hours. The demarcation ring forms by the end of the first day. Its absence or initial signs is an absolute sign of newborn status. Attention: in putrefaction and artificial respiration the gastrointestinal test may give a false positive, so it is not recommended. Question: how long did the infant live?

Quick questions. Question 1: according to the World Health Organization criterion, what length and weight make an infant non-viable? Question 2: how many hours must an infant live for hyaline membranes to appear in the pulmonary alveoli? Question 3: after at least how many hours does secondary atelectasis of the lungs develop? Question 4: name three signs indicating that the infant was cared for: clothing, cord, cleaning or a mass in the stomach.

t: Causes of fetal and newborn death: antenatal and intranatal
n: Now antenatal and intranatal death. Death in these periods is mostly non-violent; death of the newborn falls in the postnatal period. Antenatal death is most often due to intrauterine asphyxia; in the examination the placenta and cord are also examined. In the antenatal period the cause may be pathology of the placenta and cord, as well as maternal illness, toxaemia and malformation. In the intranatal period, with a narrow pelvis and a large fetus, fractures of the parietal and frontal bones are seen; if the mother assists with her hand, abrasions and bruises appear on the face and neck. In birth trauma the skull bones are fractured and there is haemorrhage into the brain, but no external injury is formed.

t: Fetal and newborn death: periods and types
n: Let us consider the periods of fetal and newborn death. Fetal death is either antenatal, that is, before delivery, or intranatal, that is, during delivery. Death of a newborn occurs in the postnatal period, that is, after delivery, and from the paediatric point of view in the early neonatal period. Non-violent death can occur in the ante-, intra- and postnatal periods; violent death is observed mainly in the postnatal period. Violent death of the fetus, that is, in the ante- and intranatal periods, is very rare.

t: Antenatal death: placental and umbilical causes
n: Antenatal non-violent death is mostly due to intrauterine asphyxia. The cause may lie in the placenta: placenta praevia, infarction or premature separation. Other causes lie in the cord: compression, wrapping around the neck or a true knot in it. For this reason, besides the fetal body, the placenta and cord are also examined. The body shows signs of rapidly occurring death, aspiration of amniotic fluid and a large amount of meconium in the fluid.

t: Postnatal violent death: active and passive
n: Postnatal violent death is active or passive. Violent death is observed mainly in the postnatal period. In the active method, action is taken against the infant: strangulation, obstruction of breathing, drowning, as well as compression of the chest and abdomen, injury, fire. In the passive method the infant is left without care: external bleeding if the cord is not tied, hypothermia, starvation. For law enforcement bodies what matters is not whether it was active or passive, but in every case the precise cause of death. Antenatal violent death is rare; it is associated with injury or poisoning of the mother.

Features of examining the body. The first stage is external examination: length, weight, head and chest dimensions, the placenta and cord are examined. The second stage is internal examination, chest and abdomen. Here the incision begins not from the chin but from the lower lip, and the umbilical vessels are preserved. In the third stage, windows are opened in the skull bones, in the vault. The fourth stage is the tests: the flotation test of the lungs and intestine. At the end, material is taken for histological and forensic biological examination.

t: Examination of the placenta and cord
n: Examination of the placenta and cord. The placenta submitted with the body is examined carefully: weight, shape, dimensions, margins and surfaces, the condition of the tissue. The cord is also examined: length, thickness, moistness, glistening, presence of a knot. Gestational age can also be determined from cord length and placental weight; in Table 10.1, for month X, 50 cm and 500 g. For histological examination, besides the internal organs, pieces are also taken from the placenta and cord.

t: Case analysis 6: cause of death and mechanism of injury
n: Case analysis. In a woman with a narrow pelvis, labour was prolonged. On the body of the newborn there is a radial fracture of the parietal bone and haemorrhage in the tentorium cerebelli, with no external wound. Question: are these injuries consistent with birth trauma? In birth trauma no external wound is formed, and fractures are most often in the parietal and frontal bones. Comparison: if the woman in labour helps herself with her hand, abrasions, bruises and a tear at the corner of the mouth appear in the face and neck region of the fetus. Attention: traces of birth trauma and of maternal assistance are not the same. For law enforcement bodies what matters is not active or passive killing, but the precise cause of death.

Review questions. 1–2: what questions are put for resolution in the examination of the body of a newborn? How does the concept of newborn status differ in forensic medicine? 3–4: list the signs of newborn status. Which signs are absolute, that is, of absolutely reliable character? 5–6: in the lung test, how can inhaled air be distinguished from putrefactive gas? How is the lung test carried out in secondary atelectasis? To test yourself, compare your answers with sections 10.1–10.3 and reread what is missing.

Let us summarise. Newborn status in forensic medicine is the first 24 hours. Live birth is decided mainly by whether the infant breathed: through tests and microscopy. Gestational age is determined by anthropometry, formulae and ossification centres. An infant less than 25 cm long and weighing less than 500 g is non-viable. Duration of life is assessed by the ring, meconium, hyaline membrane and the spread of air. Signs of care: swaddling, a tied cord, a clean body, milk in the stomach. Causes of death: in the antenatal period intrauterine asphyxia, in the intranatal period birth trauma, in the postnatal period prematurity, malformation or violence, that is, active and passive killing.
